uncertainty_flags: Lexical similarity metric is provided only for Romance languages; generalization to other families unclear and not quantified with correlation statistics
Portuguese shows anomalous performance in Fig. 2 (lower than expected given 89% similarity); authors attribute to 'lemma overlap' but do not fully resolve with controlled analysis
Northern Sami results show weak transfer even from related languages, suggesting relatedness alone is insufficient; authors note ongoing analysis but provide no resolution in current paper
Zero-shot accuracy is very low (0.01–0.14 for most pairs); practical utility and generalization to non-Romance families unclear
One-shot accuracy varies widely (0.00–0.44); only closely related pairs achieve >0.20; threshold for 'sufficiently related' not defined
Ciphering experiment shows Arabic is not purely regularization: performance varies with sample size and ciphering condition, suggesting partial transfer even for unrelated languages
Fixed hyperparameters across all languages and pairs; language-specific tuning might yield substantially different results and affect comparative claims
Claim that 'similar embeddings for similar characters have been learned' is inferred, not directly demonstrated via embedding analysis
Transfer across scripts works 'not as well' than within-script transfer; magnitude of degradation not quantified
Edit distance improvements are secondary to accuracy; practical significance unclear
One exception to transfer viability: ET→SME at 200 samples shows transfer equal to baseline; cause not explained
Subtag coverage assumption: footnote acknowledges language-specific subtag usage but does not quantify misalignment with UNIMORPH schema
Zero-shot setup constrains generalization: model has seen individual subtags; true zero-shot would require unseen subtags
Monolingual baseline at 50 samples achieves 0.00 accuracy for Romance, which is suspiciously low and may reflect data sparsity rather than true baseline
alternative_interpretations: Portuguese anomaly in Fig. 2 may reflect not lemma overlap but differences in morphological complexity or paradigm structure between Portuguese and other Romance languages, which lexical similarity alone does not capture.

Northern Sami weak results may indicate that linguistic distance (measured by phylogenetic distance or WALS features) is a better predictor of transfer than lexical similarity, suggesting the paper's relatedness metric is incomplete.

Fixed hyperparameters may systematically disadvantage morphologically complex languages (e.g., Uralic, Semitic) that might benefit from larger hidden dimensions, inflating apparent transfer effectiveness for Romance languages.

Ciphering experiment may not cleanly separate transfer from regularization because structural patterns (suffix-based inflection) persist even in ciphered data; the distinction between 'true transfer' and 'structural learning' may be artificial.

Character-level cross-script transfer may reflect not learned shared representations but rather the model's ability to learn language-specific character embeddings that happen to be useful for both scripts, without explicit cross-script alignment.

Zero-shot and one-shot results may be inflated by the constraint that 'no two training samples belong to the same lemma', which artificially limits generalization difficulty; real few-shot scenarios might have different distributions.

Language relatedness may be a necessary but not sufficient condition for transfer; other factors (morphological complexity, paradigm size, data quality) may be equally important but are not investigated.

The 58% accuracy improvement claim may be misleading because it highlights the maximum improvement (CA→ES at 50 samples) rather than typical improvement; median or mean improvement across all pairs would be more representative.
transparency_notes: This review prioritizes evidence-based claim verification over binary accept/reject judgments, following the assigned epistemic variant (evidence-and-uncertainty-first).
Uncertainty flags are explicitly separated from methodological flaws; sparse precedent in retrieved literature is treated as a possible innovation signal rather than automatic weakness.

Prior-stage digests from four reviewers (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive) are integrated to provide hierarchical context; this review builds on and extends their analyses.

Retrieved literature (Snyder & Barzilay 2008, Johnson et al. 2016, Ha et al. 2016, Kann & Schütze 2016b) provides comparable works but does not directly address the paper's core claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor; this gap is noted.
Reviewer guidelines retrieved from ARR corpus emphasize consistency, bias reduction, and clarity; this review applies those principles to claim verification.

Counterfactual reasoning is used to assess conditions under which claims could be valid: e.g., 'Under what conditions could language relatedness alone predict transfer effectiveness?' (Answer: if morphological structure correlates perfectly with lexical similarity, which the Portuguese anomaly contradicts).
Novelty risk is distinguished from methodological flaw: e.g., the ciphering ablation is novel and clever (low novelty risk) but empirically ambiguous (moderate methodological flaw).

Confidence levels reflect both evidence strength and uncertainty: high confidence claims (e.g., transfer viability) are well-supported by Table 3; medium confidence claims (e.g., language relatedness correlation) lack quantitative evidence; low confidence claims (e.g., character-level shared representations) are inferred rather than demonstrated.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The application of multi-task learning with parameter sharing to cross-lingual morphological transfer is novel in the morphology domain, though the architecture closely follows Johnson et al. (2016) in MT. The ciphering ablation to distinguish transfer from regularization is a creative methodological contribution. However, novelty does not guarantee validity: the core claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor are not fully supported by the evidence provided.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If lexical similarity metric were formally defined and computed for all 21 language pairs, and if correlation coefficient (Pearson r or Spearman ρ) were reported, the language relatedness claim would be substantially stronger.
If Portuguese anomaly were resolved through controlled experiments (e.g., excluding overlapping lemmata), the relatedness-performance correlation would be more convincing.

If Northern Sami results were analyzed in detail (linguistic distance, morphological complexity, data quality), the claim that 'relatedness is necessary for transfer' would be better supported or refined.
If zero-shot and one-shot results were validated on downstream tasks (MT, parsing), their practical utility would be clearer and the feasibility claim would be more meaningful.

If character-level cross-script transfer were demonstrated via embedding analysis (cosine similarity, t-SNE visualization), the claim about learned shared representations would be direct rather than inferred.
If hyperparameter sensitivity were tested across language families, comparative claims about transfer effectiveness would be more robust.
If ciphering experiment were complemented by alternative ablations (random tag shuffling, character permutation), the transfer vs. regularization distinction would be cleaner.

novelty_lenses.lens: Incremental novelty (application of existing techniques to new domain)
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper applies multi-task learning with parameter sharing (Johnson et al. 2016, Ha et al. 2016) to morphological paradigm completion, a straightforward extension of prior work in MT. The architecture (encoder-decoder RNN with language tags) is not novel. However, the systematic empirical evaluation across 21 language pairs and the investigation of language relatedness as a transfer predictor provide incremental contributions to understanding cross-lingual transfer in morphology.
evidence: Section 3: Architecture closely follows Kann and Schütze (2016b) for monolingual case and Johnson et al. (2016) for multilingual case
Section 6: 'we train a single model on input augmented with an explicit encoding of the language (similar to (Johnson et al., 2016))'
Contribution is primarily empirical (21 language pairs, 4 families) rather than methodological (no novel architecture or algorithm)
uncertainty_flags: Ciphering ablation is a novel methodological contribution, though empirically ambiguous
Investigation of language relatedness as transfer predictor is novel in morphology domain, though not surprising conceptually

novelty_lenses.lens: Disruptive novelty (fundamentally new approach or insight)
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper does not introduce fundamentally new concepts or approaches. The core insight—that language relatedness predicts transfer effectiveness—is intuitive and well-established in linguistics. The ciphering ablation is clever but does not fundamentally change understanding of cross-lingual transfer. The paper makes incremental progress on a specific task (paradigm completion) rather than introducing new transfer mechanisms or theoretical insights.
evidence: Section 2.1: 'we conjecture that transfer of inflectional morphology is only viable among related languages'—this is a straightforward linguistic intuition, not a novel insight
Section 5.1: Results confirm expected patterns (related languages transfer better), without surprising findings
No novel transfer mechanisms or theoretical frameworks introduced
uncertainty_flags: Ciphering experiment provides novel evidence for regularization vs. transfer distinction, though not perfectly clean
Zero-shot and one-shot learning results are interesting but weak and limited to Romance

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound (0.55) reflects significant methodological concerns: lexical similarity metric incompletely defined, Portuguese anomaly unresolved, Northern Sami results unexplained, fixed hyperparameters, and ciphering ambiguity. These issues weaken confidence in the central claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor. Upper bound (0.75) reflects strengths: comprehensive empirical evaluation across 21 pairs and 4 families, clear problem formulation, clever ablation design, and consistent patterns across most language pairs. The paper makes solid incremental contributions but has notable analytical gaps that prevent higher confidence. Confidence is medium overall: the core claims are partially supported but not fully validated.

consensus_findings: Cross-lingual transfer of inflectional morphology is viable via parameter sharing in encoder-decoder RNNs; evidence is strong for closely related language pairs (Romance, Bulgarian→Macedonian, Finnish→Estonian) with up to 58% accuracy improvement, but one exception (ET→SME at 200 samples) and weak Northern Sami results suggest limitations.

Language relatedness (measured by lexical similarity and linguistic proximity) correlates with transfer effectiveness; pattern is consistent across Romance, Slavic, and Uralic families, but correlation is observed qualitatively rather than quantified statistically, and Portuguese shows anomalous underperformance.

Unrelated languages (Arabic) provide regularization benefits distinct from true morphological transfer; ciphering ablation shows Portuguese drops dramatically (0.48→0.09 at 50 samples) while Arabic remains stable (0.54→0.56), supporting regularization hypothesis, though authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish, complicating the distinction.

Zero-shot and one-shot morphological generation are feasible for closely related languages but with low absolute accuracy; Portuguese→Spanish achieves 0.44 one-shot and 0.14 zero-shot accuracy, but results are limited to Romance languages and practical utility is unclear.

Character-level models can learn shared representations across different writing systems (Latin/Cyrillic), though transfer works 'not as well' across scripts than within-script; claim is inferred from performance patterns rather than directly demonstrated via embedding analysis.

Methodological approach (parameter sharing with language tags) is straightforward and reproducible; architecture is well-motivated and clearly described, enabling reproducibility and practical implementation.
disagreements: Strength of language relatedness as transfer predictor: Structure analyst (reviewer_1) notes correlation is 'observed but not quantified'; methodology auditor (reviewer_2) emphasizes lack of correlation coefficient; novelty assessor incremental (reviewer_3) treats as 'solid but constrained'; novelty assessor disruptive (reviewer_4) calls it 'unquantified'; claim verifier (reviewer_5) flags as 'major' methodological flaw. Consensus: correlation exists but is not statistically validated.

Practical utility of zero-shot/one-shot results: Structure analyst views as 'non-trivial result'; methodology auditor questions 'practical utility'; novelty assessor incremental notes 'weak and their practical utility is unclear'; novelty assessor disruptive emphasizes 'very low' accuracy; claim verifier flags as 'moderate' concern. Consensus: feasibility is demonstrated but practical significance is uncertain.

Severity of Portuguese anomaly: Structure analyst treats as 'moderate' concern; methodology auditor as 'moderate'; novelty assessor incremental as 'minor'; novelty assessor disruptive as 'moderate'; claim verifier as 'major'. Consensus: anomaly is significant and unresolved, weakening the relatedness hypothesis.

Novelty assessment: Structure analyst rates as 'moderate incremental'; methodology auditor as 'low novelty'; novelty assessor incremental as 'moderate incremental'; novelty assessor disruptive as 'not disruptive'; claim verifier notes 'moderate incremental novelty'. Consensus: methodological novelty is limited; empirical contribution is solid.

Ciphering ablation quality: Structure analyst views as 'clever' and 'well-motivated'; methodology auditor notes 'imperfect' separation; novelty assessor incremental calls it 'clever but imperfect'; novelty assessor disruptive emphasizes 'empirically ambiguous'; claim verifier flags as 'moderate' methodological flaw. Consensus: ablation is conceptually sound but empirically imperfect.
uncertainty_hotspots: Lexical similarity metric generalization: Metric is formally defined and quantified only for Romance languages (Tab. 2); generalization to Slavic, Uralic, and Semitic families is qualitative ('Bulgarian is closer to Macedonian') without quantitative support. All reviewers flag this as a major gap limiting the generalizability of the language relatedness hypothesis.

Portuguese anomaly resolution: Portuguese shows lower-than-expected performance (lower than French despite 89% vs. 75% lexical similarity). Authors attribute to 'lemma overlap' but provide only post-hoc analysis in footnote. All reviewers identify this as unresolved, weakening the relatedness-performance correlation claim.

Northern Sami weak results: Northern Sami shows very weak transfer even from related languages (0.01–0.02 at 50 samples). Authors acknowledge this contradicts the transfer viability claim but defer detailed analysis to future work (Footnote 4). All reviewers flag this as incomplete analysis that undermines the main claims.

Ciphering experiment interpretation: Ciphering shows Portuguese drops dramatically (0.48→0.09) while Arabic is stable (0.54→0.56), supporting regularization hypothesis. However, authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish, and ciphered Portuguese (0.09) still outperforms ciphered Arabic (0.02), suggesting structural knowledge persists. All reviewers note the distinction between transfer and regularization is not absolute.

Zero-shot accuracy practical utility: Zero-shot accuracy ranges from 0.01–0.14 for most pairs. While the paper claims 'feasibility,' absolute performance is very low. All reviewers question practical utility and note results are limited to Romance languages.

Fixed hyperparameters across all languages: Paper uses identical hyperparameters (100 hidden units, 300 embedding dimensions, 300 epochs, ADADELTA) for all 21 language pairs without language-specific tuning or sensitivity analysis. All reviewers flag this as a potential source of bias, particularly for morphologically complex languages (Uralic, Semitic).

Character-level cross-script transfer claim: Paper claims 'similar embeddings for similar characters have been learned' across Latin and Cyrillic scripts, but provides no embedding analysis (t-SNE, cosine similarity). All reviewers note this is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

Monolingual baseline at 50 samples: Monolingual Spanish achieves 0.00 accuracy at 50 samples, which is suspiciously low. Claim verifier flags this as potentially artificially weak, inflating apparent transfer improvements. Other reviewers do not address this directly.
model_diversity_effects: Structure analyst (logical-coherence-first) emphasizes coherence gaps in the argument chain, particularly the unvalidated assumptions about parameter sharing sufficiency and UNIMORPH schema universality. This lens reveals that the paper's reasoning relies on several untested assumptions that could undermine the conclusions.

Methodology auditor (reproducibility-and-validity-first) focuses on methodological rigor, flagging lack of statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. This lens reveals that empirical claims lack the quantitative validation needed for strong conclusions.

Novelty assessor incremental (incremental-contribution lens) treats the paper as an application of existing techniques to a new domain, emphasizing that methodological novelty is limited but empirical breadth is solid. This lens contextualizes the work as incremental progress rather than fundamental innovation.

Novelty assessor disruptive (disruptive-thinking lens) questions whether the paper challenges fundamental assumptions about morphological transfer or introduces new conceptual frameworks. This lens reveals that the core insight (language relatedness matters) is intuitive and expected, not surprising.

Claim verifier (evidence-and-uncertainty-first) systematically evaluates each claim against evidence, distinguishing between well-supported claims (transfer viability for related pairs), partially supported claims (language relatedness correlation), and weakly supported claims (character-level cross-script learning). This lens provides granular assessment of claim validity.

Model diversity reveals that different cognitive roles prioritize different aspects: structure analyst focuses on logical coherence, methodology auditor on empirical rigor, novelty assessors on conceptual innovation, and claim verifier on evidence quality. These perspectives collectively identify gaps that no single reviewer would fully capture.
meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes solid incremental contributions to cross-lingual morphological transfer but exhibits significant analytical gaps that weaken the central claims. The core finding—that language relatedness predicts transfer effectiveness—is well-demonstrated for closely related Romance language pairs but incompletely validated across other language families. Key issues for editorial decision: (1) Lexical similarity metric is incompletely defined and only quantified for Romance languages; generalization to other families is qualitative. (2) Portuguese anomaly (89% similarity yet lower-than-expected performance) is acknowledged but not fully resolved, undermining the relatedness hypothesis. (3) Northern Sami results contradict the transfer viability claim; analysis is deferred to future work. (4) Fixed hyperparameters across all languages may disadvantage certain pairs; no sensitivity analysis provided. (5) Ciphering ablation is clever but does not cleanly separate transfer from regularization; authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish. (6) Zero-shot and one-shot results are weak (0.01–0.14 zero-shot, 0.00–0.44 one-shot) and limited to Romance; practical utility is unclear. (7) Character-level cross-script transfer claim is inferred rather than demonstrated via embedding analysis. The paper is suitable for publication in a specialized venue (morphology, low-resource NLP) but would benefit from addressing the analytical gaps before acceptance at a top-tier venue. Recommend: (A) Require quantitative analysis of language relatedness (correlation coefficient) across all language pairs; (B) Require resolution of Portuguese anomaly via controlled experiments; (C) Require completion of Northern Sami analysis; (D) Require hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; (E) Recommend (not require) downstream task validation and embedding analysis to strengthen claims. If authors address (A)–(D), confidence in the main claims would increase substantially.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a valuable empirical contribution to understanding cross-lingual morphological transfer, with comprehensive evaluation across 21 language pairs and four language families. The ciphering ablation is a clever methodological contribution. However, several analytical gaps weaken the central claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor. To strengthen the paper: (1) Formally define the lexical similarity metric and compute it for all 21 language pairs (not just Romance). Report Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficient between lexical similarity and transfer performance. This would quantify the relatedness-performance relationship and enable statistical validation. (2) Resolve the Portuguese anomaly through controlled experiments: quantify lemma overlap between Portuguese-Spanish and other Romance pairs; rerun experiments with lemma overlap controlled; report whether Portuguese performance improves and whether the relatedness correlation strengthens. (3) Complete the Northern Sami analysis (currently deferred in Footnote 4): quantify linguistic distance between Northern Sami and source languages; analyze error patterns; determine whether weak results reflect insufficient relatedness or other factors (morphological complexity, data quality, paradigm sparsity). (4) Conduct hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: test alternative hidden unit sizes (50, 100, 200, 300) and embedding dimensions (100, 300, 500) on a subset of language pairs; report whether results change substantially; discuss implications for comparative claims across families. (5) Strengthen the ciphering ablation: conduct alternative ablations (random tag shuffling, character permutation) to test robustness of the transfer vs. regularization distinction; discuss limitations of ciphering as a clean ablation. (6) Provide direct evidence for character-level cross-script transfer: extract character embeddings; compute cosine similarity between Latin and Cyrillic characters; visualize embeddings using t-SNE; compare to random baseline. (7) Extend zero-shot/one-shot experiments to other language families (Slavic, Uralic) to test generalization beyond Romance. (8) Discuss practical utility of zero-shot/one-shot results: compare to simple baselines (copy lemma, apply most frequent suffix); evaluate impact on downstream tasks (MT, parsing) if possible. (9) Provide downstream task evaluation: integrate paradigm completion predictions into a machine translation or parsing pipeline; measure impact on downstream task performance (BLEU, UAS, LAS). This would validate practical significance of improvements. (10) Acknowledge the ET→SME exception at 200 samples and investigate its cause. These revisions would substantially strengthen the paper and increase confidence in the main claims.
transparency_report: The paper is generally transparent about limitations and exceptions. Footnote 4 acknowledges incomplete analysis of Northern Sami results ('in the process of analyzing'). Footnote 6 discusses the Portuguese anomaly and provides a retraining experiment. Section 5.1 explicitly states the ET→SME exception ('With the exception of the 200 sample case of ET→SME, cross-lingual transfer is always better than the two baselines').

However, transparency could be improved in several areas: (1) Lexical similarity metric is not formally defined; only provided for Romance languages without explanation of why other families lack quantitative metrics. (2) Fixed hyperparameters are stated but not justified; no discussion of whether this choice might disadvantage certain language pairs. (3) Ciphering ablation is presented as a clean separation of transfer from regularization, but the paper acknowledges (Footnote 8) that ciphering creates ambiguous input and (Section 5.3) that Arabic shares subtags with Spanish, complicating the interpretation. (4) Zero-shot and one-shot results are presented as 'feasible' without discussing practical utility or comparing to simple baselines. (5) Monolingual baseline at 50 samples achieves 0.00 accuracy for Romance, which is suspiciously low and not discussed.
The paper does not provide code or data availability statements, limiting reproducibility. The paper mentions using data from unimorph.org but does not specify exact versions or preprocessing steps.

The paper's claim that language relatedness 'strongly' predicts transfer success is not quantified. A correlation coefficient or regression analysis would provide more transparency about the strength of the relationship.
The paper acknowledges that the UNIMORPH schema is universal but language-specific in coverage (Footnote 2), but does not quantify the impact of this mismatch on transfer performance.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts of morphological generation for low-resource languages, though this may be outside the scope of the work.
epistemic_limits: Lexical similarity as a proxy for morphological transferability: The paper assumes lexical similarity predicts morphological transfer, but this assumption is not validated. Languages with high lexical overlap but different morphological systems (e.g., English-German) might show poor transfer despite similarity. Conversely, languages with low lexical overlap but similar morphological structures might transfer better than predicted. The Portuguese anomaly suggests lexical similarity alone is insufficient.

UNIMORPH schema universality: The paper assumes the UNIMORPH schema provides a universal, language-independent set of morphological subtags suitable for all tested languages. However, Footnote 2 acknowledges that 'which subtags a language actually uses is language-specific' (e.g., Spanish does not mark animacy as Russian does). The paper does not quantify schema coverage or misalignment, limiting confidence in the universality assumption.

Parameter sharing sufficiency: The paper assumes parameter sharing in a single encoder-decoder RNN is sufficient to enable morphological knowledge transfer between languages. However, alternative architectures (e.g., separate encoders with shared decoders, attention-based language selection, adapter modules) might be more effective. The paper does not compare to these alternatives.

Low-resource setting representativeness: The paper uses 50–200 target language samples as the low-resource setting, but real low-resource languages may have different data characteristics (e.g., noisy annotations, non-standard orthography, sparse paradigms). Results may not generalize to truly low-resource settings with <50 samples or to languages with fundamentally different morphological structures.

Ciphering as a clean ablation: The ciphering experiment assumes that random character/tag substitution disrupts true transfer while preserving regularization effects. However, ciphering creates ambiguous input representations, and structural patterns (e.g., suffix-based inflection) may persist even in ciphered data, conflating transfer with structural learning. The distinction between 'true transfer' and 'structural learning' may not be absolute.

Language relatedness as a necessary and sufficient condition: The paper demonstrates that language relatedness predicts transfer effectiveness for closely related pairs, but Northern Sami results suggest relatedness is necessary but not sufficient. Other factors (morphological complexity, paradigm size, data quality, UNIMORPH schema coverage) may be equally important but are not investigated.

Generalization of findings across language families: The paper evaluates 21 language pairs across four families, but the analysis is not uniform across families. Lexical similarity is quantified only for Romance; error analysis is provided only for Romance; zero-shot/one-shot results are reported only for Romance. Generalization to other families is uncertain.

Practical significance of improvements: The paper demonstrates accuracy improvements up to 58% but does not evaluate impact on downstream tasks (MT, parsing, speech recognition). Practical significance for real-world applications is unclear.

Statistical rigor: The paper does not report confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for the main results. This limits the ability to assess the reliability and generalizability of findings.

Causality vs. correlation: The paper demonstrates that language relatedness correlates with transfer effectiveness but does not establish causality. Relatedness may be a proxy for other factors (morphological structure similarity, paradigm completeness, data quality) that directly enable transfer.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper presents a cross-lingual transfer learning approach for morphological paradigm completion using encoder-decoder RNNs with parameter sharing and language tags. The core contribution is demonstrating that morphological knowledge transfers across languages when source and target are sufficiently related, with transfer effectiveness correlating with language relatedness (measured by lexical similarity). The work evaluates 21 language pairs spanning four language families (Romance, Slavic, Uralic, Semitic) and includes three experiments: (1) transfer learning with varying target language data sizes, (2) zero-shot and one-shot learning, and (3) ciphering ablation to distinguish true transfer from regularization. The paper is methodologically sound and well-executed within its scope, with clear presentation and comprehensive empirical breadth. However, significant analytical gaps weaken the central claims: the lexical similarity metric is incompletely defined and only quantified for Romance languages; the Portuguese anomaly (89% similarity yet lower-than-expected performance) is acknowledged but unresolved; Northern Sami results contradict transfer viability claims and analysis is deferred; fixed hyperparameters across all languages may introduce bias; the ciphering ablation does not cleanly separate transfer from regularization; zero-shot and one-shot results are weak and limited to Romance; and character-level cross-script transfer claims are inferred rather than demonstrated. The methodological novelty is limited—the approach applies established multi-task learning techniques (Johnson et al. 2016, Ha et al. 2016) to morphology—but the empirical contribution is solid. The paper makes incremental progress on an important problem (low-resource morphology) but requires substantial analytical work to validate the central claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor.
strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 21 language pairs from four language families (Romance, Slavic, Uralic, Semitic), providing broad evidence for cross-lingual transfer viability and demonstrating consistent patterns across diverse morphological systems.

Clever ciphering ablation (Experiment 3) that distinguishes true morphological transfer from regularization effects, showing Portuguese drops dramatically (0.48→0.09 at 50 samples) while unrelated Arabic remains stable (0.54→0.56), supporting the regularization hypothesis.

Clear problem formulation and practical motivation: only ~200 of 7000 languages have morphological annotations; the low-resource setting (50–200 target language samples) is realistic and practically relevant.

Demonstration of zero-shot and one-shot morphological generation feasibility for closely related languages (Portuguese→Spanish achieves 0.44 one-shot, 0.14 zero-shot accuracy), extending applicability to extremely low-resource scenarios.
Straightforward and reproducible methodology: parameter sharing with language tags is simple, well-motivated, and clearly described, enabling practical implementation and reproducibility.

Systematic investigation of language relatedness effects across multiple language families, with consistent patterns showing related languages transfer better (Bulgarian best for Macedonian, Finnish best for Estonian).
Transparent acknowledgment of limitations and exceptions: Portuguese anomaly, Northern Sami weakness, and ET→SME exception are explicitly noted rather than hidden.
limitations: Lexical similarity metric is incompletely defined and only quantified for Romance languages (Tab. 2: PT 89%, CA 85%, IT 82%, FR 75% vs. ES). For Slavic, Uralic, and Semitic families, relatedness is discussed qualitatively ('Bulgarian is closer to Macedonian') without quantitative support. This limits the generalizability of the central claim that language relatedness predicts transfer effectiveness. No correlation coefficient (Pearson r or Spearman ρ) is reported between lexical similarity and transfer performance, leaving the 'strongly correlated' claim unquantified.

Portuguese anomaly in Fig. 2 is unresolved: Portuguese shows lower-than-expected performance (lower than French despite 89% vs. 75% lexical similarity), contradicting the relatedness hypothesis. Authors attribute this to 'potentially confusing overlap of lemmata' but provide only post-hoc analysis in Footnote 6 using a different dataset (3695 vs. 12,000 samples). This anomaly weakens confidence in the relatedness-performance correlation and suggests lexical similarity alone is insufficient to predict transfer success.

Northern Sami results contradict the transfer viability claim: Northern Sami shows very weak transfer even from related languages (0.01–0.02 at 50 samples, 0.05–0.20 at 200 samples), and ET→SME at 200 samples shows transfer equal to monolingual baseline (0.74 vs. 0.74). Authors acknowledge this ('For Northern Sami, transfer works least well') but defer detailed analysis to future work (Footnote 4: 'in the process of analyzing SME results in more detail'). This incomplete analysis leaves a critical gap in understanding when transfer fails despite language relatedness.
open_questions: How does the lexical similarity metric generalize beyond Romance languages? The paper provides quantitative similarity scores only for Romance pairs. Computing lexical similarity for all 21 language pairs and reporting correlation coefficients would strengthen the central claim about language relatedness as a transfer predictor. What metric should be used (Levenshtein distance, cognate overlap, ASJP distance), and how does it correlate with transfer performance across all language families?

What explains the Portuguese anomaly in Fig. 2? Portuguese has the highest lexical similarity to Spanish (89%) yet shows lower performance than Catalan (85%) and Italian (82%). Is this due to lemma overlap, morphological differences, or other factors? A controlled experiment excluding overlapping lemmata across all Romance pairs would clarify whether this is a data artifact or a genuine limitation of the relatedness hypothesis.

Why do Northern Sami results show such weak transfer despite linguistic relatedness to Finnish, Hungarian, and Estonian? Is the issue linguistic distance (Uralic languages are more distant than Romance), morphological complexity (Northern Sami has more inflectional categories), data quality, or UNIMORPH schema misalignment? Completing the deferred analysis would clarify whether relatedness is necessary but not sufficient for transfer.

How sensitive are the results to hyperparameter choices? The paper uses fixed hyperparameters (100 hidden units, 300 embedding dimensions, 300 epochs, ADADELTA) across all languages. Would language-specific tuning substantially change the relative rankings of source languages or the apparent transfer effectiveness? Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis would strengthen confidence in comparative claims.

Does the ciphering ablation cleanly separate transfer from regularization? Ciphering shows Portuguese drops dramatically (0.48→0.09) while Arabic is stable (0.54→0.56), but authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish and ciphered Portuguese (0.09) still outperforms ciphered Arabic (0.02). Do alternative ablations (random tag shuffling, character permutation) yield consistent conclusions about the transfer vs. regularization distinction?
consensus_snapshot: Cross-lingual transfer of inflectional morphology is viable via parameter sharing in encoder-decoder RNNs; evidence is strong for closely related language pairs (Romance, Bulgarian→Macedonian, Finnish→Estonian) with up to 58% accuracy improvement, but exceptions (ET→SME, Northern Sami) suggest limitations.

Language relatedness correlates with transfer effectiveness; pattern is consistent across Romance, Slavic, and Uralic families, but correlation is observed qualitatively rather than quantified statistically, and Portuguese shows anomalous underperformance.

Unrelated languages (Arabic) provide regularization benefits distinct from true morphological transfer; ciphering ablation shows Portuguese drops dramatically while Arabic remains stable, supporting regularization hypothesis, though authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish.

Zero-shot and one-shot morphological generation are feasible for closely related languages but with low absolute accuracy; Portuguese→Spanish achieves 0.44 one-shot and 0.14 zero-shot accuracy, but results are limited to Romance and practical utility is unclear.
Methodological approach (parameter sharing with language tags) is straightforward and reproducible; architecture is well-motivated and clearly described, enabling practical implementation.

Methodological novelty is limited; the approach applies established multi-task learning techniques (Johnson et al. 2016, Ha et al. 2016) to morphology without introducing novel architectural components or training procedures.
disagreement_snapshot: Strength of language relatedness as transfer predictor: Reviewers agree correlation exists but is not statistically validated. Structure analyst notes correlation is 'observed but not quantified'; methodology auditor emphasizes lack of correlation coefficient; claim verifier flags as 'major' methodological flaw. Consensus: correlation is qualitative, not quantitative.

Practical utility of zero-shot/one-shot results: Reviewers disagree on significance. Structure analyst views as 'non-trivial result'; methodology auditor questions 'practical utility'; novelty assessors emphasize 'very low' accuracy; claim verifier flags as 'moderate' concern. Consensus: feasibility is demonstrated but practical significance is uncertain.

Severity of Portuguese anomaly: Reviewers rate as 'moderate' to 'major' concern. All agree anomaly is significant and unresolved, weakening the relatedness hypothesis. Consensus: anomaly requires controlled analysis before publication.

Novelty assessment: Reviewers rate methodological novelty as 'low' to 'moderate incremental'; empirical contribution as 'solid' to 'strong'. Consensus: novelty is primarily empirical (breadth of evaluation) rather than methodological.

Ciphering ablation quality: Reviewers view as 'clever' but 'imperfect' or 'empirically ambiguous'. Consensus: ablation is conceptually sound but does not cleanly separate transfer from regularization.
uncertainty_snapshot: Lexical similarity metric generalization: Metric is formally defined and quantified only for Romance languages; generalization to Slavic, Uralic, and Semitic families is qualitative without quantitative support. All reviewers flag this as a major gap.

Portuguese anomaly resolution: Portuguese shows lower-than-expected performance despite 89% lexical similarity. Authors attribute to 'lemma overlap' but provide only post-hoc analysis in footnote. All reviewers identify this as unresolved.

Northern Sami weak results: Northern Sami shows very weak transfer even from related languages (0.01–0.02 at 50 samples). Authors defer detailed analysis to future work. All reviewers flag this as incomplete analysis undermining main claims.

Ciphering experiment interpretation: Ciphering shows Portuguese drops dramatically while Arabic is stable, supporting regularization hypothesis. However, authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish, and ciphered Portuguese still outperforms ciphered Arabic, suggesting structural knowledge persists. All reviewers note the distinction is not absolute.

Zero-shot accuracy practical utility: Zero-shot accuracy ranges from 0.01–0.14 for most pairs. While paper claims 'feasibility,' absolute performance is very low. All reviewers question practical utility.

Fixed hyperparameters across all languages: Paper uses identical hyperparameters for all 21 pairs without language-specific tuning or sensitivity analysis. All reviewers flag this as potential source of bias.

Character-level cross-script transfer claim: Paper claims 'similar embeddings for similar characters have been learned' across Latin and Cyrillic scripts, but provides no embedding analysis. All reviewers note this is inferred rather than demonstrated.

Monolingual baseline at 50 samples: Monolingual Spanish achieves 0.00 accuracy at 50 samples, which is suspiciously low. Claim verifier flags this as potentially artificially weak, inflating apparent transfer improvements.
source_trace: Lexical similarity metric definition and generalization: Tab. 2 provides Romance similarity scores; Section 4 discusses Slavic/Uralic/Semitic relatedness qualitatively; Section 5.1 states 'More closely related source languages improve performance more than distant ones' without quantification. Retrieved literature (Snyder & Barzilay 2008) on cross-lingual morphology provides precedent for relatedness-based transfer but does not quantify the relationship.

Portuguese anomaly: Fig. 2 shows Portuguese learning curves lower than expected; Section 5.1 notes 'potentially confusing overlap of lemmata'; Footnote 6 provides retraining experiment on different dataset. No controlled analysis in main text.

Northern Sami results: Tab. 3 shows ET→SME at 50 samples (0.01–0.02 accuracy) and 200 samples (0.05–0.20 accuracy); Section 5.1 states 'transfer works least well'; Footnote 4 defers analysis. No detailed investigation provided.

Ciphering ablation: Section 5.3 describes methodology; Tab. 5 shows results (PT→ES drops 0.48→0.09, AR→ES stable 0.54→0.56); Section 5.3 acknowledges 'Arabic and Spanish share subtags'; Footnote 8 notes 'ciphering creates ambiguous input'. Authors acknowledge limitations but do not fully resolve the transfer vs. regularization distinction.

Zero-shot/one-shot results: Tab. 4 provides accuracy data (PT→ES 0.44 one-shot, 0.14 zero-shot); Section 5.2 discusses feasibility; Footnote 7 notes 'model has seen the individual subtags'. Results limited to Romance languages.

Character-level cross-script transfer: Section 5.1 states 'transfer works across alphabets (although not as well)' and 'suggests that similar embeddings for similar characters have been learned'. No embedding analysis provided; claim is inferred from performance patterns.

Fixed hyperparameters: Section 5 states 'We keep hyperparameters during all experiments (and for all languages) fixed to the following values: 100 hidden units, 300 embedding dimensions, 300 epochs, ADADELTA optimizer'. No justification or sensitivity analysis provided.
Monolingual baseline: Tab. 3 shows monolingual baseline '0' achieving 0.00 accuracy for Romance at 50 samples. No discussion of why this baseline is so weak or whether it is realistic.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about limitations and exceptions. Footnote 4 acknowledges incomplete Northern Sami analysis ('in the process of analyzing'). Footnote 6 discusses Portuguese anomaly and provides retraining experiment. Section 5.1 explicitly states ET→SME exception ('With the exception of the 200 sample case of ET→SME, cross-lingual transfer is always better than the two baselines').

However, transparency could be improved: (1) Lexical similarity metric is not formally defined; only provided for Romance without explanation of why other families lack quantitative metrics. (2) Fixed hyperparameters are stated but not justified; no discussion of whether this choice might disadvantage certain language pairs. (3) Ciphering ablation is presented as clean separation but paper acknowledges (Footnote 8) that ciphering creates ambiguous input and (Section 5.3) that Arabic shares subtags with Spanish. (4) Zero-shot/one-shot results are presented as 'feasible' without discussing practical utility or comparing to simple baselines. (5) Monolingual baseline at 50 samples achieves 0.00 accuracy, which is suspiciously low and not discussed.
The paper does not provide code or data availability statements, limiting reproducibility. The paper mentions using data from unimorph.org but does not specify exact versions or preprocessing steps.

The claim that language relatedness 'strongly' predicts transfer success is not quantified. A correlation coefficient or regression analysis would provide more transparency about the strength of the relationship.
The paper acknowledges that the UNIMORPH schema is universal but language-specific in coverage (Footnote 2), but does not quantify the impact of this mismatch on transfer performance.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts of morphological generation for low-resource languages, though this may be outside the scope of the work.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes solid incremental contributions to cross-lingual morphological transfer but exhibits significant analytical gaps that weaken the central claims. The core finding—that language relatedness predicts transfer effectiveness—is well-demonstrated for closely related Romance language pairs but incompletely validated across other language families. Key issues for editorial decision: (1) Lexical similarity metric is incompletely defined and only quantified for Romance languages; generalization to other families is qualitative. (2) Portuguese anomaly (89% similarity yet lower-than-expected performance) is acknowledged but not fully resolved, undermining the relatedness hypothesis. (3) Northern Sami results contradict the transfer viability claim; analysis is deferred to future work. (4) Fixed hyperparameters across all languages may disadvantage certain pairs; no sensitivity analysis provided. (5) Ciphering ablation is clever but does not cleanly separate transfer from regularization; authors acknowledge Arabic shares subtags with Spanish. (6) Zero-shot and one-shot results are weak (0.01–0.14 zero-shot, 0.00–0.44 one-shot) and limited to Romance; practical utility is unclear. (7) Character-level cross-script transfer claim is inferred rather than demonstrated via embedding analysis. The paper is suitable for publication in a specialized venue (morphology, low-resource NLP) but would benefit from addressing the analytical gaps before acceptance at a top-tier venue. Recommend: (A) Require quantitative analysis of language relatedness (correlation coefficient) across all language pairs; (B) Require resolution of Portuguese anomaly via controlled experiments; (C) Require completion of Northern Sami analysis; (D) Require hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; (E) Recommend (not require) downstream task validation and embedding analysis to strengthen claims. If authors address (A)–(D), confidence in the main claims would increase substantially.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a valuable empirical contribution to understanding cross-lingual morphological transfer, with comprehensive evaluation across 21 language pairs and four language families. The ciphering ablation is a clever methodological contribution. However, several analytical gaps weaken the central claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor. To strengthen the paper: (1) Formally define the lexical similarity metric and compute it for all 21 language pairs (not just Romance). Report Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficient between lexical similarity and transfer performance. This would quantify the relatedness-performance relationship and enable statistical validation. (2) Resolve the Portuguese anomaly through controlled experiments: quantify lemma overlap between Portuguese-Spanish and other Romance pairs; rerun experiments with lemma overlap controlled; report whether Portuguese performance improves and whether the relatedness correlation strengthens. (3) Complete the Northern Sami analysis (currently deferred in Footnote 4): quantify linguistic distance between Northern Sami and source languages; analyze error patterns; determine whether weak results reflect insufficient relatedness or other factors (morphological complexity, data quality, paradigm sparsity). (4) Conduct hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: test alternative hidden unit sizes (50, 100, 200, 300) and embedding dimensions (100, 300, 500) on a subset of language pairs; report whether results change substantially; discuss implications for comparative claims across families. (5) Strengthen the ciphering ablation: conduct alternative ablations (random tag shuffling, character permutation) to test robustness of the transfer vs. regularization distinction; discuss limitations of ciphering as a clean ablation. (6) Provide direct evidence for character-level cross-script transfer: extract character embeddings; compute cosine similarity between Latin and Cyrillic characters; visualize embeddings using t-SNE; compare to random baseline. (7) Extend zero-shot/one-shot experiments to other language families (Slavic, Uralic) to test generalization beyond Romance. (8) Discuss practical utility of zero-shot/one-shot results: compare to simple baselines (copy lemma, apply most frequent suffix); evaluate impact on downstream tasks (MT, parsing) if possible. (9) Provide downstream task evaluation: integrate paradigm completion predictions into a machine translation or parsing pipeline; measure impact on downstream task performance (BLEU, UAS, LAS). This would validate practical significance of improvements. (10) Acknowledge the ET→SME exception at 200 samples and investigate its cause.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper presents a cross-lingual transfer learning approach for morphological paradigm completion using encoder-decoder RNNs with parameter sharing and language tags. The work evaluates 21 language pairs spanning four language families and demonstrates that morphological transfer is viable for related languages, with transfer effectiveness correlating with language relatedness. The paper makes incremental methodological contributions (applying multi-task learning to morphology) with solid empirical breadth (21 pairs, 4 families) but exhibits significant analytical gaps that weaken the central claims about language relatedness as a transfer predictor.

Strengths:
- Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 21 language pairs from four language families (Romance, Slavic, Uralic, Semitic), providing broad evidence for cross-lingual transfer viability and demonstrating consistent patterns across diverse morphological systems.
- Clever ciphering ablation (Experiment 3) that distinguishes true morphological transfer from regularization effects, showing Portuguese drops dramatically (0.48→0.09 at 50 samples) while unrelated Arabic remains stable (0.54→0.56).
- Clear problem formulation and practical motivation: only ~200 of 7000 languages have morphological annotations; the low-resource setting (50–200 target language samples) is realistic and practically relevant.
- Demonstration of zero-shot and one-shot morphological generation feasibility for closely related languages (Portuguese→Spanish achieves 0.44 one-shot, 0.14 zero-shot accuracy).
- Straightforward and reproducible methodology: parameter sharing with language tags is simple, well-motivated, and clearly described, enabling practical implementation.
- Systematic investigation of language relatedness effects across multiple language families, with consistent patterns showing related languages transfer better.
- Transparent acknowledgment of limitations and exceptions: Portuguese anomaly, Northern Sami weakness, and ET→SME exception are explicitly noted.

Limitations:
- Lexical similarity metric is incompletely defined and only quantified for Romance languages (Tab. 2: PT 89%, CA 85%, IT 82%, FR 75% vs. ES). For Slavic, Uralic, and Semitic families, relatedness is discussed qualitatively ('Bulgarian is closer to Macedonian') without quantitative support. This limits the generalizability of the central claim that language relatedness predicts transfer effectiveness. No correlation coefficient (Pearson r or Spearman ρ) is reported between lexical similarity and transfer performance, leaving the 'strongly correlated' claim unquantified.
- Portuguese anomaly in Fig. 2 is unresolved: Portuguese shows lower-than-expected performance (lower than French despite 89% vs. 75% lexical similarity), contradicting the relatedness hypothesis. Authors attribute this to 'potentially confusing overlap of lemmata' but provide only post-hoc analysis in Footnote 6 using a different dataset (3695 vs. 12,000 samples). This anomaly weakens confidence in the relatedness-performance correlation and suggests lexical similarity alone is insufficient to predict transfer success.

Open Questions:
- How does the lexical similarity metric generalize beyond Romance languages? Computing lexical similarity for all 21 language pairs and reporting correlation coefficients would strengthen the central claim about language relatedness as a transfer predictor.
- What explains the Portuguese anomaly in Fig. 2? A controlled experiment excluding overlapping lemmata across all Romance pairs would clarify whether this is a data artifact or a genuine limitation of the relatedness hypothesis.
- Why do Northern Sami results show such weak transfer despite linguistic relatedness to Finnish, Hungarian, and Estonian? Completing the deferred analysis would clarify whether relatedness is necessary but not sufficient for transfer.
- How sensitive are the results to hyperparameter choices? Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis would strengthen confidence in comparative claims across language families.
- Does the ciphering ablation cleanly separate transfer from regularization? Do alternative ablations (random tag shuffling, character permutation) yield consistent conclusions about the transfer vs. regularization distinction?

Transparency:
The paper is generally transparent about limitations and exceptions, explicitly noting the Portuguese anomaly, Northern Sami weakness, and ET→SME exception. However, transparency could be improved by: (1) formally defining the lexical similarity metric and explaining why it is only quantified for Romance languages; (2) justifying the choice of fixed hyperparameters across all languages; (3) more prominently discussing the limitations of the ciphering ablation (ambiguous input, shared subtags); (4) discussing practical utility of zero-shot/one-shot results; (5) explaining why the monolingual baseline at 50 samples achieves 0.00 accuracy. The paper does not provide code or data availability statements, limiting reproducibility.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
